sentences.text: Aletopelta was originally estimated to reach 6 meters in length, but later analysis by Gregory S. Paul revised these dimensions to 5 meters and a weight of 2 tonnes.
This dinosaur is characterized by wide teeth, a femur longer than the tibia and ulna, three metatarsals, shoulder spikes, and a mosaic of small polygonal osteoderms at the hip level.
Arbour and Currie (2015) diagnosed the genus based on hexagonal pelvic osteoderms forming a semi-continuous sheet and a specific fusion pattern in the neck armor.
The holotype carcass was washed into the sea, sank upside down, and became a miniature reef inhabited by marine invertebrates.
Sharks and marine invertebrates scavenged the carcass, leaving hollow long bones and pits on the armor.
The holotype skeleton was discovered in 1987 during construction work near Carlsbad, California, where a ditch for a sewage pipe uncovered the remains.
The skeleton was first described in 1996 by Deméré and Coombs and formally named in 2001 by Ford and Kirkland.
Its wide teeth suggest a diet capable of processing tough vegetation or small prey.
The femur being much longer than the tibia and ulna indicates a specific adaptation in its hindlimb structure.
Ford and Kirkland (2001) classified Aletopelta as a distinct genus and species within the family Ankylosauridae, placing it there rather than Nodosauridae based on its unique armor arrangement.
The fossil record for Aletopelta spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Vickaryous et al. (2004) considered Aletopelta a nomen dubium due to insufficient diagnostic features.
Arbour and Currie (2015) argued for the validity of the genus based on new characteristics and rejected the subfamily Stegopeltinae.
While often placed as a basal ankylosaurid, some studies suggest it may be the most basal nodosaurid.
